items.stem: Which of the following best describes "enzyme–substrate specificity"?
options: The rate at the start of a reaction, found from the gradient of the tangent to a product–time curve at time zero
Metabolic reactions that build larger molecules from smaller ones, such as protein synthesis
An instrument that measures the absorbance or transmission of light by a solution, used to follow reactions that change colour
The property that each enzyme catalyses only one reaction or a small group of reactions because only substrates with a complementary shape and chemistry bind to the active site
items.answer: The property that each enzyme catalyses only one reaction or a small group of reactions because only substrates with a complementary shape and chemistry bind to the active site
items.markingKey: D. "enzyme–substrate specificity" is the property that each enzyme catalyses only one reaction or a small group of reactions because only substrates with a complementary shape and chemistry bind to the active site.

items.stem: Distinguish between the lock-and-key model and the induced-fit model.
items.answer: In the lock-and-key model the active site is rigid and exactly complementary to the substrate; in the induced-fit model the active site changes shape on binding to fit the substrate closely and strain its bonds.
items.markingKey: In the lock-and-key model the active site is rigid and exactly complementary to the substrate; in the induced-fit model the active site changes shape on binding to fit the substrate closely and strain its bonds. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain the induced-fit model of enzyme action.
items.answer: The active site is not exactly complementary to the substrate; as the substrate binds, the enzyme (and substrate) change shape slightly so they fit closely; this strains bonds in the substrate, lowering the activation energy and promoting the reaction; products are then released and the active site returns to its original shape. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The active site is not exactly complementary to the substrate; as the substrate binds, the enzyme (and substrate) change shape slightly so they fit closely; this strains bonds in the substrate, lowering the activation energy and promoting the reaction; products are then released and the active site returns to its original shape. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "All enzymes work inside cells." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Some enzymes are extracellular, such as digestive enzymes secreted into the gut and enzymes secreted by fungi onto their food.
items.markingKey: Some enzymes are extracellular, such as digestive enzymes secreted into the gut and enzymes secreted by fungi onto their food. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Discs of potato tissue containing catalase were placed in hydrogen peroxide solution at different temperatures. The volume of oxygen collected in 2 minutes was measured.

Temperature / °C | Volume of O₂ in 2 min / cm³
10 | 2.5
20 | 5.3
30 | 10.2
40 | 21.5
50 | 11.2
60 | 1.9

(a) Calculate the mean rate of oxygen production at 40 °C in cm³ min⁻¹. [1]
(b) State the temperature at which the highest rate was recorded. [1]
(c) Calculate the percentage increase in the volume of oxygen between 10 °C and 30 °C. [2]

The volume of oxygen released when a peroxidase from turnip was added to hydrogen peroxide was measured with a gas syringe every 30 s.

Time / s | Volume of O₂ / cm³
0 | 0.0
30 | 9.8
60 | 15.8
90 | 19.4
120 | 21.6
150 | 22.9
180 | 23.7

(a) Calculate the mean rate of oxygen production over the first 30 s in cm³ min⁻¹. [2]
(b) Calculate the mean rate between 120 s and 180 s in cm³ min⁻¹. [1]
(c) Explain why the rate decreases during the experiment. [2]
(d) Calculate the percentage of the final volume that had been produced after 60 s. [1]
items.answer: (a) 19.6 cm³ min⁻¹ (b) 2.1 cm³ min⁻¹ (c) Hydrogen peroxide (substrate) is used up, so its concentration falls; fewer enzyme–substrate collisions per unit time. (d) 67 %
items.markingKey: (a) [2] 9.8 cm³ in 0.5 min (M1) = 19.6 cm³ min⁻¹ (A1). (b) [1] (23.7 − 21.6) cm³ in 1 min = 2.1 cm³ min⁻¹ (A1). (c) [2] Substrate used up (A1); fewer collisions / ES complexes (A1). (d) [1] 15.8/23.7 × 100 = 67 % (A1).

items.stem: Explain how the structure of enzymes allows them to act as specific catalysts.
items.answer: Globular proteins; tertiary structure; active site formed by few amino acids; complementary shape/chemistry to substrate; specificity; induced fit – shape change, strain on bonds; lowers activation energy; collision and orientation; products released; enzyme unchanged; denaturation/mutation alter active site.
items.markingKey: Globular proteins; tertiary structure; active site formed by few amino acids; complementary shape/chemistry to substrate; specificity; induced fit – shape change, strain on bonds; lowers activation energy; collision and orientation; products released; enzyme unchanged; denaturation/mutation alter active site.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "The induced-fit model has completely replaced the lock-and-key model."
items.answer: Induced fit is the more accurate model, but it builds on rather than discards the complementarity central to lock-and-key; models are refined over time.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: induced fit explains why active sites change shape and how bonds are strained; it explains broad specificity of some enzymes. Arguments against: the lock-and-key idea of complementarity is still central and useful in teaching; some enzymes change shape very little on binding. Supported judgement: Induced fit is the more accurate model, but it builds on rather than discards the complementarity central to lock-and-key; models are refined over time. Markbands (7 marks): Markscheme points: award 1 mark for each valid, relevant point up to the maximum; points must be linked and explained, not listed. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem: Which part of an enzyme determines its specificity?
options: the total number of amino acids
the shape and chemical properties of the active site
the length of the polypeptide chain only
items.answer: the shape and chemical properties of the active site
items.markingKey: C. Only complementary substrates bind.

items.stem: Why does an enzyme catalyse only one type of reaction?
options: Its active site is complementary in shape and chemistry to one specific substrate.
It contains many different active sites.
It is used up in the reaction.
It changes the equilibrium of the reaction.
items.answer: Its active site is complementary in shape and chemistry to one specific substrate.
items.markingKey: A. Specificity.

items.stem: Why can an enzyme catalyse only a specific reaction?
options: Only a substrate with a complementary shape and chemistry can bind to the active site.
All substrates have the same shape.
Enzymes are made of only one amino acid.
Enzymes form covalent bonds with every molecule.
items.answer: Only a substrate with a complementary shape and chemistry can bind to the active site.
items.markingKey: A. Specificity arises from the 3D structure.

items.stem:
The initial rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction (arbitrary units) was measured at different substrate concentrations, with and without a fixed concentration of inhibitor X.

(b) Calculate the percentage inhibition at 32 mmol dm⁻³ substrate. [1]
Outline one way in which lactase used to produce lactose-free milk shows enzyme–substrate specificity and the use of enzymes.
items.answer: Immobilised lactase hydrolyses lactose into glucose and galactose as milk flows past. Lactase acts only on lactose, so other milk components are unchanged; immobilisation allows reuse.
items.markingKey: Context (Immobilised lactase hydrolyses lactose into glucose and galactose as milk flows past.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Lactase acts only on lactose, so other milk components are unchanged; immobilisation allows reuse. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to enzyme–substrate specificity and the use of enzymes.

Which of the following best describes "substrate concentration"?
options: The region of an enzyme, formed by a few amino acids, to which the substrate binds and where catalysis occurs
The amount of substrate per unit volume, which affects the frequency of enzyme–substrate collisions
A molecule with a shape similar to the substrate that binds to the active site, blocking substrate binding
The pH at which an enzyme has its highest activity
items.answer: The amount of substrate per unit volume, which affects the frequency of enzyme–substrate collisions
items.markingKey: B. "substrate concentration" is the amount of substrate per unit volume, which affects the frequency of enzyme–substrate collisions.

items.stem: Why does pH affect enzyme activity?
options: Changes in H⁺ concentration alter ionic and hydrogen bonds in the enzyme, changing the active site shape.
items.answer: Changes in H⁺ concentration alter ionic and hydrogen bonds in the enzyme, changing the active site shape.
items.markingKey: A. Charge on R groups.

items.stem: Explain the effect of increasing temperature on the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction.
items.answer: As temperature rises, enzyme and substrate molecules gain kinetic energy and collide more often with sufficient energy, so rate increases up to the optimum; above the optimum, vibrations break hydrogen and ionic bonds in the enzyme, changing the active site shape (denaturation), so fewer substrates bind and the rate falls steeply.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: As temperature rises, enzyme and substrate molecules gain kinetic energy and collide more often with sufficient energy, so rate increases up to the optimum; above the optimum, vibrations break hydrogen and ionic bonds in the enzyme, changing the active site shape (denaturation), so fewer substrates bind and the rate falls steeply. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Pepsin is placed in a solution of pH 7. What is the most likely result?
options: Little or no activity because the pH is far from its optimum.
items.answer: Little or no activity because the pH is far from its optimum.
items.markingKey: C. Pepsin works at pH about 2.

items.stem: Outline one way in which pepsin and trypsin in the human digestive system shows the effect of pH on enzyme activity.
items.answer: Pepsin works in the acidic stomach (pH about 2) and trypsin in the alkaline small intestine (pH about 8). Each has an active site whose R-group charges suit its environment, so each enzyme is most active at a different pH.
items.markingKey: Context (Pepsin works in the acidic stomach (pH about 2) and trypsin in the alkaline small intestine (pH about 8).) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Each has an active site whose R-group charges suit its environment, so each enzyme is most active at a different pH. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the effect of pH on enzyme activity.

items.stem: A student claims: "At low temperatures enzymes are denatured." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Low temperatures reduce kinetic energy and collisions, slowing the reaction, but do not usually denature enzymes; activity returns on warming.
items.markingKey: Low temperatures reduce kinetic energy and collisions, slowing the reaction, but do not usually denature enzymes; activity returns on warming. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Temperature is the most important factor affecting enzyme activity in the human body."
items.answer: Because body temperature is held constant, enzyme activity is mainly controlled by substrate/enzyme concentration, pH in compartments and inhibition; temperature matters most when homeostasis fails.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: temperature affects every enzyme and fever can denature proteins; body temperature is tightly regulated because of this. Arguments against: pH varies more between compartments (stomach vs intestine) than temperature; substrate and enzyme concentrations and inhibitors regulate most pathways day to day. Supported judgement: Because body temperature is held constant, enzyme activity is mainly controlled by substrate/enzyme concentration, pH in compartments and inhibition; temperature matters most when homeostasis fails.

items.stem: Explain the effects of temperature, pH and substrate concentration on enzyme activity.
items.answer: Temperature: kinetic energy, collisions, optimum, denaturation above; pH: ionisation of R groups, optimum, denaturation at extremes; substrate concentration: rate rises then plateaus at saturation (Vmax); graphs described; examples pepsin/trypsin.
items.markingKey: Temperature: kinetic energy, collisions, optimum, denaturation above; pH: ionisation of R groups, optimum, denaturation at extremes; substrate concentration: rate rises then plateaus at saturation (Vmax); graphs described; examples pepsin/trypsin.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A permanent change in the shape of an enzyme’s active site, caused by high temperature or extreme pH, so it can no longer bind its substrate"?
items.answer: denaturation
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of denaturation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the effect of temperature below the optimum and the effect of temperature above the optimum.
items.answer: Below the optimum, increasing temperature increases kinetic energy and collision frequency, raising the rate; above it, increasing temperature denatures the enzyme, lowering the rate.
items.markingKey: Below the optimum, increasing temperature increases kinetic energy and collision frequency, raising the rate; above it, increasing temperature denatures the enzyme, lowering the rate. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Why does the rate of an enzyme reaction fall rapidly above the optimum temperature?
options: Bonds maintaining the active site break, so the enzyme is denatured.
items.answer: Bonds maintaining the active site break, so the enzyme is denatured.
items.markingKey: A. Hydrogen and ionic bonds break.

items.stem: Pepsin works in the stomach and trypsin in the small intestine. Which is most likely?
options: Pepsin has a low optimum pH (about 2) and trypsin an optimum pH of about 8.
Trypsin has an optimum pH of 2.
Both have an optimum pH of 7.
Pepsin has an optimum pH of 8.
items.answer: Pepsin has a low optimum pH (about 2) and trypsin an optimum pH of about 8.
items.markingKey: A. Matched to location.

items.stem: What does the gradient of a graph of product formed against time represent?
items.answer: the rate of reaction
items.markingKey: the rate of reaction. Rate = change in product/time.

items.stem: Explain why a tangent is drawn to a product–time curve to find the initial rate.
items.answer: The curve is steepest at the start and becomes less steep as substrate is used up; a tangent at t = 0 gives the gradient (rate) under the starting conditions only.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The curve is steepest at the start and becomes less steep as substrate is used up; a tangent at t = 0 gives the gradient (rate) under the starting conditions only. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Why is the initial rate measured when comparing enzyme activity under different conditions?
options: At the start substrate concentration is known and not yet limiting, so rates are comparable.
items.answer: At the start substrate concentration is known and not yet limiting, so rates are comparable.
items.markingKey: B. Initial conditions are controlled.

items.stem: An enzyme produces 4.8 cm³ of gas in the first 30 s. What is the initial rate in cm³ min⁻¹?
items.markingKey: C. 4.8 ÷ 0.5 min = 9.6 cm³ min⁻¹.

items.stem: Oxygen released by catalase was 12 cm³ in the first 30 s. What is the initial rate?
items.answer: 0.40 cm³ s⁻¹

items.stem: Explain how enzymes speed up reactions and describe how the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction can be determined experimentally.
items.answer: Activation energy; energy profile diagram; enzyme lowers activation energy, not ΔG; induced fit strains bonds; methods: product (O₂ gas syringe), substrate disappearance (iodine test), colorimeter; rate = amount/time or 1/t; initial rate from tangent; repeats, controls.
items.markingKey: Activation energy; energy profile diagram; enzyme lowers activation energy, not ΔG; induced fit strains bonds; methods: product (O₂ gas syringe), substrate disappearance (iodine test), colorimeter; rate = amount/time or 1/t; initial rate from tangent; repeats, controls.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The rate at the start of a reaction, found from the gradient of the tangent to a product–time curve at time zero"?
items.answer: initial rate
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of initial rate.

items.stem: Explain the difference between initial rate and mean rate.
items.answer: Mean rate is the total change divided by total time; initial rate is the rate at the start of the reaction, found from the gradient of the tangent at t = 0 and usually higher than the mean rate.
items.markingKey: Mean rate is the total change divided by total time; initial rate is the rate at the start of the reaction, found from the gradient of the tangent at t = 0 and usually higher than the mean rate. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "A reaction that takes longer has a higher rate." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Rate is inversely proportional to time: rate = 1/t, so a longer time means a lower rate.
items.markingKey: Rate is inversely proportional to time: rate = 1/t, so a longer time means a lower rate. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With reference to catalase in liver cells, explain how it illustrates the lowering of activation energy by enzymes.
items.answer: Catalase breaks down hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen up to millions of times per second. Without the enzyme, decomposition of H₂O₂ is very slow because its activation energy is high.
items.markingKey: Context (Catalase breaks down hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen up to millions of times per second.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Without the enzyme, decomposition of H₂O₂ is very slow because its activation energy is high. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the lowering of activation energy by enzymes.

items.stem: "Measuring the time to reach an end point is a reliable way to compare enzyme activity." Discuss.
items.answer: It is acceptable for simple comparisons but continuous measurement (e.g. colorimeter or gas syringe) gives more precise, objective initial rates.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it is simple and gives a rate (1/t) for each condition; it needs only basic equipment. Arguments against: judging a colour end point by eye is subjective; it gives a mean rate rather than an initial rate. Supported judgement: It is acceptable for simple comparisons but continuous measurement (e.g. colorimeter or gas syringe) gives more precise, objective initial rates. items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A chain or cycle of enzyme-catalysed reactions in which the product of one reaction is the substrate of the next"?
items.answer: metabolic pathway
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of metabolic pathway.

items.stem: What happens to Vmax in the presence of a non-competitive inhibitor?
items.answer: It decreases.
items.markingKey: A. Effectively fewer active enzyme molecules.

items.stem: Arjun writes: "End-product inhibition stops a metabolic pathway permanently." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: End-product inhibition is reversible: when the product concentration falls the inhibitor leaves the enzyme and the pathway resumes.
items.markingKey: End-product inhibition is reversible: when the product concentration falls the inhibitor leaves the enzyme and the pathway resumes. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Malonate resembles succinate and slows the Krebs cycle enzyme succinate dehydrogenase, but its effect disappears at high succinate concentrations. What type of inhibitor is malonate?
items.answer: competitive
items.markingKey: B. Effect overcome by substrate.

items.stem: Using penicillin treatment of bacterial infections as an example, explain mechanism-based inhibition.
items.answer: Penicillin binds covalently to transpeptidase, preventing cross-linking of peptidoglycan. Irreversible binding permanently inactivates the enzyme so bacterial walls are weakened.
items.markingKey: Context (Penicillin binds covalently to transpeptidase, preventing cross-linking of peptidoglycan.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Irreversible binding permanently inactivates the enzyme so bacterial walls are weakened. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to mechanism-based inhibition.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Enzyme inhibitors are the most important tool in modern drug development."
items.answer: Enzyme inhibitors are a major class of drugs and structural biology makes them central, but they are one of several important approaches.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: many important drugs are enzyme inhibitors: statins, penicillin, protease inhibitors for HIV, aspirin; knowledge of active site structure allows rational drug design. Arguments against: many drugs act on receptors, ion channels or as replacement hormones; resistance can evolve, e.g. bacterial β-lactamases. Supported judgement: Enzyme inhibitors are a major class of drugs and structural biology makes them central, but they are one of several important approaches.

items.stem: Which statement describes non-competitive inhibition?
options: the inhibitor binds the active site
increasing substrate concentration does not overcome the inhibition
items.answer: increasing substrate concentration does not overcome the inhibition
items.markingKey: C. Fewer functional enzyme molecules.

items.stem: Explain how penicillin kills bacteria.
items.answer: Penicillin binds irreversibly (covalently) to the active site of transpeptidase, which cross-links peptidoglycan; new cell walls are weak; bacteria burst by osmosis as they grow – mechanism-based inhibition.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Penicillin binds irreversibly (covalently) to the active site of transpeptidase, which cross-links peptidoglycan; new cell walls are weak; bacteria burst by osmosis as they grow – mechanism-based inhibition. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Cyanide binds to cytochrome c oxidase away from the active site. What kind of inhibitor is it?
items.answer: non-competitive
items.markingKey: B. Allosteric binding.

items.stem: A graph of rate against substrate concentration with an inhibitor reaches the same maximum as without it, but more slowly. Which inhibitor type is shown?
items.answer: competitive
items.markingKey: A. Vmax unchanged.

items.stem: Distinguish between competitive and non-competitive inhibition and explain how end-product inhibition regulates metabolic pathways.
items.answer: Competitive: active site, substrate-like, overcome by substrate, Vmax same; non-competitive: allosteric site, shape change, Vmax reduced; graphs; examples statins/malonate, cyanide; end-product: isoleucine inhibits threonine deaminase, negative feedback, reversible, efficient; mechanism-based penicillin.
items.markingKey: Competitive: active site, substrate-like, overcome by substrate, Vmax same; non-competitive: allosteric site, shape change, Vmax reduced; graphs; examples statins/malonate, cyanide; end-product: isoleucine inhibits threonine deaminase, negative feedback, reversible, efficient; mechanism-based penicillin.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Metabolic reactions that build larger molecules from smaller ones, such as protein synthesis"?
items.answer: anabolism
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of anabolism.

items.answer: A permanent change in the shape of an enzyme’s active site, caused by high temperature or extreme pH, so it can no longer bind its substrate

items.stem: How do enzymes increase the rate of reactions?
options: by raising the temperature of the cell
by supplying energy to the substrate
items.answer: by lowering the activation energy
items.markingKey: D. Less energy needed to reach the transition state.

items.stem: Why is end-product inhibition an example of negative feedback?
options: Accumulating product inhibits an early enzyme, reducing further production.
items.answer: Accumulating product inhibits an early enzyme, reducing further production.
items.markingKey: A. Self-regulation.

items.stem: Distinguish between catabolic reactions and anabolic reactions.
items.answer: Anabolic reactions synthesise complex molecules from simpler ones and require energy (e.g. protein synthesis); catabolic reactions break complex molecules into simpler ones and release energy (e.g. respiration, digestion).
items.markingKey: Anabolic reactions synthesise complex molecules from simpler ones and require energy (e.g. protein synthesis); catabolic reactions break complex molecules into simpler ones and release energy (e.g. respiration, digestion). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Why do enzymes increase the rate of reaction?

They lower the activation energy of the reaction.
items.answer: They lower the activation energy of the reaction.
items.markingKey: D. Alternative pathway.

items.stem: Distinguish between competitive inhibition and non-competitive inhibition.
items.answer: Competitive inhibitors bind the active site and are overcome by high substrate concentration (Vmax unchanged); non-competitive inhibitors bind an allosteric site, change the enzyme’s shape and are not overcome by substrate (Vmax reduced).
items.markingKey: Competitive inhibitors bind the active site and are overcome by high substrate concentration (Vmax unchanged); non-competitive inhibitors bind an allosteric site, change the enzyme’s shape and are not overcome by substrate (Vmax reduced). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Why is metabolism described as a web of interdependent reactions?
options: All reactions use the same enzyme.
The product of one reaction is often the substrate of another, linking pathways.
Reactions occur only one at a time.
items.answer: The product of one reaction is often the substrate of another, linking pathways.
items.markingKey: C. Pathways branch and connect.

items.markingKey: Many inhibitors are useful: drugs such as statins and penicillin, and natural end-product inhibitors that regulate metabolism. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "The induced-fit model has completely replaced the lock-and-key model."
items.answer: Induced fit is the more accurate model, but it builds on rather than discards the complementarity central to lock-and-key; models are refined over time.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: induced fit explains why active sites change shape and how bonds are strained; it explains broad specificity of some enzymes. Arguments against: the lock-and-key idea of complementarity is still central and useful in teaching; some enzymes change shape very little on binding. Supported judgement: Induced fit is the more accurate model, but it builds on rather than discards the complementarity central to lock-and-key; models are refined over time.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Temperature is the most important factor affecting enzyme activity in the human body."
items.answer: Because body temperature is held constant, enzyme activity is mainly controlled by substrate/enzyme concentration, pH in compartments and inhibition; temperature matters most when homeostasis fails.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: temperature affects every enzyme and fever can denature proteins; body temperature is tightly regulated because of this. Arguments against: pH varies more between compartments (stomach vs intestine) than temperature; substrate and enzyme concentrations and inhibitors regulate most pathways day to day. Supported judgement: Because body temperature is held constant, enzyme activity is mainly controlled by substrate/enzyme concentration, pH in compartments and inhibition; temperature matters most when homeostasis fails. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Measuring the time to reach an end point is a reliable way to compare enzyme activity."
items.answer: It is acceptable for simple comparisons but continuous measurement (e.g. colorimeter or gas syringe) gives more precise, objective initial rates.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it is simple and gives a rate (1/t) for each condition; it needs only basic equipment. Arguments against: judging a colour end point by eye is subjective; it gives a mean rate rather than an initial rate. Supported judgement: It is acceptable for simple comparisons but continuous measurement (e.g. colorimeter or gas syringe) gives more precise, objective initial rates. items.stem:
The initial rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction (arbitrary units) was measured at different substrate concentrations, with and without a fixed concentration of inhibitor X.

Substrate / mmol dm⁻³ | Rate without X | Rate with X
1 | 18 | 7
2 | 31 | 12
4 | 46 | 18
8 | 60 | 23
16 | 72 | 28
32 | 80 | 31

(a) Calculate the percentage inhibition at 2 mmol dm⁻³ substrate. [2]
(b) Calculate the percentage inhibition at 32 mmol dm⁻³ substrate. [1]
(c) Deduce, with a reason, whether X is a competitive or a non-competitive inhibitor. [2]
(d) Describe the effect of substrate concentration on the rate without inhibitor. [2]
(e) Explain how a non-competitive inhibitor reduces the rate of reaction. [2]
(f) Predict the maximum rate with inhibitor X at very high substrate concentration. [1]
(g) State one variable that must be kept constant. [1]
(h) Explain why the initial rate, rather than the rate after several minutes, was measured. [2]
items.answer: (a) 61 % (b) 61 % (c) non-competitive: the percentage inhibition stays about the same at all substrate concentrations, so extra substrate does not overcome it (d) Rate increases steeply at low substrate concentrations, then more slowly, approaching a maximum as active sites become saturated. (e) It binds to an allosteric site, changing the shape of the active site so the substrate cannot bind or react. (f) Lower than without X (≈ 35 units) (g) Temperature, pH, enzyme concentration, inhibitor concentration. (h) Substrate concentration falls and product accumulates as the reaction proceeds, so only the initial rate reflects the stated substrate concentration.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (31 − 12)/31 × 100 (M1) = 61 % (A1). (b) [1] (80 − 31)/80 × 100 = 61 % (A1). (c) [2] non-competitive (A1); reason from comparison of percentage inhibition (R1). (d) [2] Increase then levelling (A1); saturation explanation (R1). (e) [2] Binding site (A1); effect on substrate binding (A1). (f) [1] Correct prediction consistent with inhibitor type (A1). (g) [1] Any one (A1). (h) [2] Substrate depletion (A1); valid comparison (A1).

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "enzyme–substrate specificity".
items.answer: The property that each enzyme catalyses only one reaction or a small group of reactions because only substrates with a complementary shape and chemistry bind to the active site
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the property that each enzyme catalyses only one reaction or a small group of reactions because only substrates with a complementary shape and chemistry bind to the active site. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Why does increasing temperature from 10 °C to 30 °C increase the rate of an enzyme reaction?
options: molecules move faster, so collisions between enzyme and substrate are more frequent
items.answer: molecules move faster, so collisions between enzyme and substrate are more frequent
items.markingKey: B. Kinetic energy rises.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "initial rate"?
options: An instrument that measures the absorbance or transmission of light by a solution, used to follow reactions that change colour
The minimum energy that reacting molecules must have for a reaction to occur; enzymes lower it
A permanent change in the shape of an enzyme’s active site, caused by high temperature or extreme pH, so it can no longer bind its substrate
The rate at the start of a reaction, found from the gradient of the tangent to a product–time curve at time zero
items.answer: The rate at the start of a reaction, found from the gradient of the tangent to a product–time curve at time zero
items.markingKey: D. "initial rate" is the rate at the start of a reaction, found from the gradient of the tangent to a product–time curve at time zero.

items.stem: Explain the difference between non-competitive inhibition and competitive inhibition.
items.answer: Competitive inhibitors bind the active site and are overcome by high substrate concentration (Vmax unchanged); non-competitive inhibitors bind an allosteric site, change the enzyme’s shape and are not overcome by substrate (Vmax reduced).
items.markingKey: Competitive inhibitors bind the active site and are overcome by high substrate concentration (Vmax unchanged); non-competitive inhibitors bind an allosteric site, change the enzyme’s shape and are not overcome by substrate (Vmax reduced). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Isabel writes: "All enzymes work inside cells." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Some enzymes are extracellular, such as digestive enzymes secreted into the gut and enzymes secreted by fungi onto their food.
items.markingKey: Some enzymes are extracellular, such as digestive enzymes secreted into the gut and enzymes secreted by fungi onto their food. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Why does the rate of an enzyme reaction level off at high substrate concentrations?
options: All active sites are occupied, so enzyme concentration becomes limiting.
items.answer: All active sites are occupied, so enzyme concentration becomes limiting.
items.markingKey: B. Saturation.

items.stem: Which statement about the energy profile of an enzyme-catalysed reaction is correct?
options: The peak (transition state) is lower than in the uncatalysed reaction.
items.answer: The peak (transition state) is lower than in the uncatalysed reaction.
items.markingKey: A. Lower activation energy barrier.

items.stem: Why can a competitive inhibitor’s effect be overcome by more substrate?
options: Substrate and inhibitor compete for the same active site; more substrate wins more often.
items.answer: Substrate and inhibitor compete for the same active site; more substrate wins more often.
items.markingKey: A. Competition.

items.stem: Why is the induced-fit model considered better than the lock-and-key model?
options: It explains how the active site changes shape slightly on binding, stressing bonds in the substrate.
It shows enzymes have no active site.
It shows the substrate changes the enzyme permanently.
items.answer: It explains how the active site changes shape slightly on binding, stressing bonds in the substrate.
items.markingKey: A. Flexible active site.

items.stem: "All enzymes have an optimum pH of 7." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Optimum pH varies: pepsin about 2, trypsin about 8, salivary amylase about 7.
items.markingKey: Optimum pH varies: pepsin about 2, trypsin about 8, salivary amylase about 7. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
The volume of oxygen released when catalase extracted from celery was added to hydrogen peroxide was measured with a gas syringe every 30 s.

Time / s | Volume of O₂ / cm³
0 | 0.0
30 | 8.0
60 | 13.0
90 | 16.1
120 | 18.1
150 | 19.4
180 | 20.2

(a) Calculate the mean rate of oxygen production over the first 30 s in cm³ min⁻¹. [2]
(b) Calculate the mean rate between 120 s and 180 s in cm³ min⁻¹. [1]
(c) Explain why the rate decreases during the experiment. [2]
items.answer: (a) 16.0 cm³ min⁻¹ (b) 2.1 cm³ min⁻¹ (c) Hydrogen peroxide (substrate) is used up, so its concentration falls; fewer enzyme–substrate collisions per unit time.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] 8.0 cm³ in 0.5 min (M1) = 16.0 cm³ min⁻¹ (A1). (b) [1] (20.2 − 18.1) cm³ in 1 min = 2.1 cm³ min⁻¹ (A1). (c) [2] Substrate used up (A1); fewer collisions / ES complexes (A1).

items.stem: A mutation changes an amino acid far from the active site, yet enzyme activity is lost. What is the best explanation?
options: The substrate binds to that amino acid.
The change altered the tertiary structure, changing the shape of the active site.
items.answer: The change altered the tertiary structure, changing the shape of the active site.
items.markingKey: C. Folding links distant residues to the active site.

items.stem: Doubling enzyme concentration, with excess substrate, has which effect on initial rate?
items.answer: It approximately doubles.
items.markingKey: A. More active sites.

items.stem: The time taken for a filter-paper disc soaked in catalase to rise to the surface of hydrogen peroxide was 270 s at 1 % enzyme and 129 s at 2 % enzyme. Calculate the rate (1000/t, in s⁻¹) under each condition and the percentage increase in rate.
Outline one way in which statins prescribed to lower blood cholesterol shows competitive inhibition.
items.answer: Statins bind to the active site of HMG-CoA reductase in the liver, reducing cholesterol synthesis. The drug resembles the substrate and competes for the active site.
items.markingKey: Context (Statins bind to the active site of HMG-CoA reductase in the liver, reducing cholesterol synthesis.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The drug resembles the substrate and competes for the active site. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to competitive inhibition.

items.stem: "Enzyme inhibitors are the most important tool in modern drug development." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Enzyme inhibitors are a major class of drugs and structural biology makes them central, but they are one of several important approaches.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: many important drugs are enzyme inhibitors: statins, penicillin, protease inhibitors for HIV, aspirin; knowledge of active site structure allows rational drug design. Arguments against: many drugs act on receptors, ion channels or as replacement hormones; resistance can evolve, e.g. bacterial β-lactamases. Supported judgement: Enzyme inhibitors are a major class of drugs and structural biology makes them central, but they are one of several important approaches.
